why: Two independent effects both make \(g\) largest at the poles. First, the Earth is not a perfect sphere but an ellipsoid bulged at the equator: the polar radius is about 6356 km against an equatorial radius of about 6378 km, and since \(g = \dfrac{GM}{R^{2}}\) the smaller radius gives the larger value — about 9.91 m/s\(^{2}\) at the pole against about 9.84 m/s\(^{2}\) at the equator on radius alone. Second, the Earth's rotation subtracts a centrifugal term that is largest at the equator and exactly zero on the axis of rotation, that is at the poles, pulling the equatorial figure down further to roughly 9.80 m/s\(^{2}\). The equator therefore loses on both counts. At the centre of the Earth the acceleration is \(g_{d} = g\left(1 - \dfrac{d}{R}\right)\) with \(d = R\), so it vanishes there. Just above the surface \(g_{h} = \dfrac{gR^{2}}{(R+h)^{2}}\), which decreases as the height grows, so no point above the surface can beat the surface directly beneath it. The largest value is reached at the pole of the Earth.

Inside the Earth only the material lying below the observer contributes to the gravitational pull; the spherical shell above exerts no net force on anything inside it. That gives the depth relation \(g_{d} = g\left(1 - \dfrac{d}{R}\right)\). At the centre the depth equals the whole radius, \(d = R\), so \(g_{d} = g(1 - 1) = 0\) and the weight \(W = mg_{d}\) is nil. Physically the surrounding matter pulls the particle equally in every direction and those pulls cancel by symmetry. Note that the particle's MASS is unchanged — mass is an intrinsic property of the body — while weight is the gravitational force on it, and it is the force that disappears. An infinite weight would need the force to diverge, which never happens inside a uniform sphere. It is not the same as at other places either, since \(g_{d}\) falls linearly from its full surface value to nothing as the centre is approached; and it is certainly not greater than at the poles, where \(g\) takes its largest surface value of all.

Gravitational potential is negative everywhere and rises towards nought at infinity, so asking for its MINIMUM means asking where it is most negative. Outside the Earth \(V = -\dfrac{GM}{r}\), while inside it \(V = -\dfrac{GM(3R^{2} - r^{2})}{2R^{3}}\). Putting \(r = 0\) gives the value at the centre, \(V = -\dfrac{3GM}{2R}\), which is one and a half times as negative as the surface value \(-\dfrac{GM}{R}\). Numerically, for the Earth, that is about \(-9.38 \times 10^{7}\) J/kg at the centre against about \(-6.25 \times 10^{7}\) J/kg at the surface, so the surface is not the minimum. Any interior point that is not the centre lies strictly between those two figures — at half the radius it is about \(-8.60 \times 10^{7}\) J/kg — so it cannot be the minimum either. At infinite distance \(V = 0\), which is the LARGEST value the potential ever attains rather than the smallest. The potential is therefore least at the centre of the Earth.

For a satellite in a circular orbit of radius \(r\) about a planet of mass \(M\), the kinetic energy is \(\dfrac{GMm}{2r}\), the potential energy is \(-\dfrac{GMm}{r}\), and the total energy is their sum, \(-\dfrac{GMm}{2r}\). Binding energy is the minimum energy that must be supplied to release the satellite from the planet's gravitational influence, so it equals the magnitude of that total energy, \(\dfrac{GMm}{2r}\). Comparing the two expressions, the kinetic energy and the binding energy have exactly the same magnitude. With a binding energy of \(3 \times 10^{9}\) J the kinetic energy is therefore \(3 \times 10^{9}\) J, and it is positive. The three rejected values are each a different quantity drawn from the same problem: \(6 \times 10^{9}\) J is the magnitude of the potential energy, which is twice the binding energy; \(-3 \times 10^{9}\) J is the total energy; and \(-6 \times 10^{9}\) J is the potential energy itself. Kinetic energy is \(\tfrac{1}{2}m\mathrm{v}^{2}\) and can never be negative, which disposes of both negative values at once.
